result: The manuscript describes the historical development, organizational structure, and guiding philosophy of the BRAIN Initiative. Claims include the 2014 launch from a 2013 Presidential directive, guidance by an advisory committee, the Brain 2025 report with seven priority areas, special Congressional appropriation enabling flexibility, the core philosophy of understanding the brain as a complex system necessary for treating disorders, and the organizational structure including the split of systems neuroscience from technology development in FY2015.
evaluation: All three reviewers describe the manuscript as a 'convincing summary' or 'convincing description' of the BRAIN Initiative's historical development and structure. No reviewer questions these foundational, historical, and organizational claims. The reviewers accept the manuscript's documentation of the program's origins and structure without critique.

result: The manuscript describes the BRAIN Circuits Program ecosystem of funding mechanisms, including the staged funding format (2/3-year exploratory followed by 5-year expanded awards), three major research tracks (targeted single-lab, team-research, and human neuroscience), requirements for multi-scale approaches, and total expenditures of approximately $1B over 10 years with balanced funding between small-lab ($384M) and team-research ($403M) approaches.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the manuscript as containing 'a fair bit of documentation' and providing 'specific funding mechanisms' and 'examples of grants funded.' The quantitative funding data and program structure are presented as factual documentation that reviewers accept without challenge. The reviewers note the paper's value in allowing readers to 'parse what this BRAIN program funded.'

result: The manuscript describes the Theories, Models, and Methods (TMM) computational neuroscience program, designed as a 'tool building' program to develop and disseminate computational tools while avoiding replication of existing NSF/NIH programs. The TMM program required end-user evaluation and experimental validation, later adding requirements for cellular and sub-second temporal resolution. The program represented 7% of total expenditures ($65M), with tool popularity measured by GitHub metrics showing high engagement for calcium imaging methods, encoding/decoding tools, and statistical methods.
evaluation: Reviewers note the manuscript 'conduct[s] analyses of...the popularity of some tools developed' and contains documentation allowing readers to understand program outputs. The description of the TMM program structure and its tool outputs is accepted as part of the comprehensive documentation of BRAIN Initiative activities. No reviewer questions the TMM program design or impact metrics.

result: The manuscript describes the Basic Behavioral Quantification and Synchronization (BBQS) program initiated in FY2023 to improve high-content, high-temporal resolution behavioral measures. The program includes staged funding tracts for human and organismal behavior with different review processes, but the authors acknowledge it is premature to assess overall impacts.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the manuscript's description of this newly launched program without critique. The authors' explicit acknowledgment that impact assessment is premature aligns with the reviewers' acceptance of the manuscript as documentation of program structure rather than requiring demonstrated outcomes for all initiatives.

result: The manuscript claims the BRAIN Circuits Program created a more than fourfold accumulation of investment compared to NIH baseline funding in systems and computational neuroscience. NIH baseline funding grew at 4.2% per year while BRAIN investments climbed at an additional 12.5% per year, with the actual increment for basic, disease-agnostic discovery substantially higher than 4× when accounting for the composition of baseline funding.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the manuscript as conducting 'analyses of the impact on overall funding in Systems and Computational Neuroscience' and note the authors 'have improved the presentation...by performing additional analyses.' The funding impact analysis is accepted as part of the convincing documentation of the program's scale and influence on the field.

result: The manuscript presents bibliometric productivity measures across funding mechanisms, including median publications, citations, and Relative Citation Ratio (RCR) per award. Key findings include: TeamBCP showing much higher publication rates than Parent R01s and substantially more citations than other programs; BRAIN awards generally having higher median RCR than Parent R01s; budget efficiency highest for TeamBCP, TMM, Parent R01, and eROH programs; and all programs accumulating publications and citations at a 'healthy rate of return' with 'impressive impacts.'
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note the manuscript 'conduct[s] analyses of...the raw and field normalized bibliographic impact of the work' and describe these analyses as part of what makes the manuscript 'convincing.' One reviewer specifically states the authors 'have improved the presentation...by performing additional analyses,' suggesting the bibliometric data strengthens the manuscript's claims about program impact.

result: The manuscript presents advancement rates from exploratory to elaborated awards: 13% for R34 to R01 (characterized as 'high-risk/high-reward'), 59% for exploratory TeamBCP, and 73% for exploratory ROH. When including advancement to any NIH award, rates rose to 30%, 76%, and 73% respectively. The authors acknowledge these transition metrics are incomplete measures of impact, particularly for tool-building awards that may have broad community use without generating traditional citations or subsequent awards.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the advancement rate data as part of the manuscript's comprehensive documentation. The authors' explicit acknowledgment of the limitations of these metrics demonstrates appropriate scientific caution that reviewers implicitly accept by not challenging these claims. The data is presented as one of multiple impact measures rather than the sole indicator of success.

result: The manuscript presents Altmetric scores as measures of public impact and media attention for BRAIN-funded research. High-popularity topics include sleep/wake behaviors, maternal behaviors, SARS-CoV-2 and anosmia, discovery of a possible fourth meningeal membrane, neural circuitry of maternal responses, speech/language decoding for prostheses, and anxiety activity in brain hormonal axes. Some fundamental neuroscience projects showed early translational impact.
evaluation: Reviewers note the manuscript 'conduct[s] analyses of...the social media impact of the funded work,' accepting this as part of the comprehensive impact assessment. The Altmetric data is presented alongside bibliometric measures to provide multiple perspectives on program impact, which reviewers accept as appropriate documentation of public engagement with BRAIN-funded research.

result: The manuscript describes the evolution and scale of the team-research approach, from the initial 2014 3-year 'Integrated Approaches' program through the 2017 5-year TeamBCP and 2018 exploratory eTeamBCP. Total expenditures for FY2014-2023 were $118.7M for eTeamBCP and $280.7M for TeamBCP, balanced with $348M for parallel small-project awards. In FY2023, team-science expenditures were $129.4M (19% of total BRAIN Initiative expenditures).
evaluation: Reviewers describe the manuscript as providing 'specific funding mechanisms utilized' and note the authors 'draw on a wealth of real-life experience reviewing, funding, and administering large team projects.' The detailed financial documentation and program evolution are accepted as factual descriptions of the team-science investment strategy.

result: The manuscript describes TeamBCP consortia structure and advancement outcomes. All awardees joined leadership and data science consortia that produced topic maps showing broad portfolio coverage across systems and behaviors, with modeling efforts spanning broad scales. Of 17 original 3-year awards (2014-15), 59% advanced to 5-year TeamBCP and 76% to any NIH award. Of 20 total TeamBCP, 55% came from novel sources including 15% from non-NIH funding. The manuscript compares these rates favorably to NIH RPG success rates (21.3%), NIMH Conte Centers (73%), and P01 programs (71%), concluding the staged funding strategy was 'highly successful.'
evaluation: Reviewers note the authors 'are able to draw on a wealth of real-life experience reviewing, funding, and administering large team projects, and assessing how well they achieve their goals.' The advancement rate data and comparative analysis are accepted as evidence of program success. No reviewer questions the interpretation that these rates demonstrate effectiveness of the team-science approach.

result: The manuscript claims the program has facilitated cultural change in systems neuroscience through multidisciplinary team-science approaches. Evidence includes: demographic survey showing 31% of respondents in computational fields, 42% from physics/engineering backgrounds, 5% neuroethicists; projects spanning multiple scales, disciplines, and species; consortia building research communities sharing best practices; expanded training environments producing multifaceted trainees; and recognition of team science challenges including management, authorship, and credit assignment that are monitored through site visits and trainee working groups.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the manuscript as 'convincing' and note the authors 'draw on a wealth of real-life experience' with team projects. The cultural impact claims are supported by multiple forms of evidence (survey data, consortium activities, trainee outcomes) that reviewers accept as demonstrating the program's influence on research practices. The acknowledgment of challenges alongside successes adds credibility that reviewers implicitly accept.

result: The manuscript describes data science infrastructure and its effectiveness. Required data science cores promoted flexible solutions for sharing complex data across disciplines, formats, and scales. Site visits revealed these cores effectively addressed unique data sharing challenges without burdening research staff productivity. The 'bottom-up' project-specific approach complements 'top-down' BRAIN data archives. However, self-evaluation identified needs for improved standards in organizing, documenting, and sharing data/software, with particular challenges in recruiting and incentivizing data science efforts for early-career scientists.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the manuscript's balanced assessment of data science infrastructure, including both successes and areas for improvement. The authors' acknowledgment of limitations through self-evaluation data demonstrates appropriate scientific assessment that reviewers implicitly support by not challenging these claims. The description of data management approaches is accepted as part of the comprehensive program documentation.

result: The manuscript describes annual site visits for TeamBCP awards using External Advisory Boards (EAB) composed of NIH/NSF Program Officers, scientists from other BRAIN awards, and invited scientists. EABs assess progress, offer critique, explore opportunities, and highlight achievements. Site visits emphasizing SWOT (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) format have 'proven to be one of the most valuable factors' in the TeamBCP program for scientific goals and progress management.
evaluation: Reviewers note the authors 'draw on a wealth of real-life experience reviewing, funding, and administering large team projects, and assessing how well they achieve their goals.' The description of site visit processes and their value is accepted as part of the authors' documented experience with program management. No reviewer questions the effectiveness claims for this oversight mechanism.

result: The manuscript describes cross-species and cross-scale research approaches. Species studied include Drosophila, zebrafish, rodents, primates, nudebranch, octopus, voles, bats, and humans, revealing conserved and diverse neural mechanisms. Extensive cross-scale modeling demonstrates the power of quantitative approaches, leading to enhanced collaboration between theorists and experimentalists. Survey data shows diverse disciplinary representation (Engineering 28%, Psychology/Behavioral Science, Biology, Physiology 18-28%). The next generation of scientists is characterized as more multifaceted, able to move across scales and speak multiple scientific languages, with theorists and experimentalists similarly engaged in data science training.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the manuscript as 'convincing' in its documentation of the program's scope and impact. The cross-species and cross-disciplinary data are accepted as evidence of the program's breadth and its influence on training the next generation of neuroscientists. Survey data supporting these claims is accepted without challenge as part of the comprehensive program assessment.

result: The manuscript argues that team-research programs succeed by fostering collective efforts beyond individual projects, requiring a shift from traditional single-PI competitive review mindsets to emphasis on synergy, co-publication, and collective capacity. The funding program rubric and review criteria drive an ecosystem transcending single-PI limitations. Awardees have engaged 'more adventurous and necessarily collaborative programs of high impact' on topics transcending individual Institute interests. The manuscript concludes the TeamBCP has been 'a leading agent for changing the culture' of neuroscience research and recommends it continue as an enduring model, with the BRAIN Initiative participating in a NASEM consensus study on team science.
evaluation: Reviewers describe the manuscript as 'convincing' and note it has been 'improved with respect to clarity' in revision. The cultural impact claims and recommendations are accepted as reasonable conclusions from the documented evidence. Reviewers' characterization of the manuscript as providing 'an important summary' suggests they accept the authors' interpretation of the program's transformative influence on neuroscience research culture.

result: The manuscript's overarching conclusions claim the BRAIN Initiative Circuits Program has 'substantially advanced and changed the landscape' of research funding in systems and computational neuroscience. Supporting evidence includes: ~$1B investment over 10 years achieving more than fourfold increase in funding rate compared to pre-BRAIN decade; raw and normalized citation indices showing 'impressive measures of scientific impact' with particularly high performance by TeamBCP; staged funding strategy being 'highly effective'; and production of 'fiscally efficient, high-impact discovery' across broad research topics. These conclusions are supported by informal polls of Program Directors and recognition across NIH neuroscience Institute priorities.
evaluation: All three reviewers characterize the manuscript as 'convincing' in its summary and description of the BRAIN Initiative's impact. Reviewers note the manuscript provides 'an important summary' that is 'of particular value at this moment in history.' The comprehensive quantitative evidence (funding data, bibliometrics, advancement rates) combined with qualitative assessments are accepted as supporting the conclusion of substantial impact on the neuroscience funding landscape. No reviewer challenges the magnitude or significance of the claimed impacts.

result: The manuscript describes methodological approaches for data collection and analysis, including curation of baseline systems neuroscience awards to match BRAIN mechanisms, extraction of budget and application data from NIH FASTR, publications from iCITE, and calculation of bibliometric measures using iCITE and custom Python scripts.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the methodological descriptions without critique. The manuscript's documentation of data sources and analytical approaches is treated as appropriate transparency for the quantitative analyses presented. No reviewer questions the validity or appropriateness of the methods used to assess program impact.
